criteria.definition: Official one-command installer covering the primary OS tiers (Linux, macOS, Windows) with no manual archive unpacking required.
Toolchain or its official installer is available through mainstream OS-native package managers (apt, dnf, pacman, Homebrew, Chocolatey/winget, etc.).
An official or de-facto standard version/toolchain manager exists for switching release channels and pinning per-project versions.
Installer/toolchain manager simplifies acquiring additional cross-compilation targets/platforms out of the box.
Checksums/signatures and archived historical installer/toolchain versions are available for reproducible or offline installs.
Clarity and discoverability of the official install documentation across platforms.

frozen_rubric.description: Objective 0-100 rubric applied identically to all 10 languages for Installation / Distribution Experience. Sub-criteria and point weights are frozen before scoring any language.

citations: It makes cross-compiling simpler with binary builds of the standard library for common platforms.
cross_target_support.rationale: rustup ships binary builds of the standard library for common platforms, making cross-compilation target acquisition a single 'rustup target add' operation.

citations: On Windows, go to https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install and follow the instructions for installing Rust.
Linux users should generally install GCC or Clang, according to their distribution’s documentation.
doc_clarity.rationale: Official install docs (rust-lang.org/tools/install, the Rustup book, and the Rust Book's installation chapter) give explicit per-OS steps, verification commands, and pointers to build-tool prerequisites (e.g. MSVC linker on Windows), though a native C toolchain prerequisite on some platforms is an extra manual step.

citations: As of 2024/12/23, this is the case for APT, homebrew and pacman.
Starting from Debian 13 (trixie) and Ubuntu 24.04 (noble), you may use apt to install rustup
Please note that Rust tools like rustc and cargo are not available via $PATH by default in this rustup distribution
native_pkg_manager_availability.rationale: As of late 2024 rustup itself (with proxies for rustc/cargo) is installable via APT, Homebrew and pacman, and rustup-init alone via DNF; Debian 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 ship apt-installable rustup. Homebrew's rustup distribution notably does not expose rustc/cargo on PATH by default, a minor rough edge.

citations: To download Rustup and install Rust, run the following in your terminal, then follow the on-screen instructions.
To install Rust, download and run rustup‑init.exe then follow the onscreen instructions.
one_step_installer.rationale: rust-lang.org provides a single curl|sh command for Unix-likes and a downloadable rustup-init.exe GUI installer for Windows, both from one official page.

citations: To get a previous version, use https://static.rust-lang.org/rustup/archive/{rustup-version}/{target-tuple}/rustup-init[.exe].
SHA-256 checksums are also available by appending .sha256 to the link.
verification_reproducibility.rationale: Archived rustup-init and toolchain builds are retrievable by exact version/date, and SHA-256 checksums are published for installer artifacts.

citations: Rustup installs The Rust Programming Language from the official release channels, enabling you to easily switch between stable, beta, and nightly compilers and keep them updated.
The most basic track the official release channels: stable, beta and nightly; but rustup can also install toolchains from the official archives, for alternate host platforms, and from local builds.
version_toolchain_manager.rationale: rustup is the official toolchain installer/manager enabling switching between stable, beta and nightly channels, per-directory toolchain overrides, and archived-version installs.

July 9, 2026 · The Rust Release Team · The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.97.0.

criteria.definition: Existence of a publicly documented, predictable release cadence/schedule.
Formal, documented backward-compatibility / non-breakage commitment for the stable channel, with mechanisms (e.g. staged compatibility testing) to enforce it.
Clear opt-in mechanism for evolving the language/edition without breaking existing code, plus a documented versioning scheme.
Deterministic versioning and availability of exact historical release artifacts for reproducible builds.
Documented maintenance/patch policy, including whether more than the newest release receives fixes (LTS-style support) or only latest.

frozen_rubric.description: Objective 0-100 rubric applied identically to all 10 languages for Toolchain Stability / Release Maturity. Language age and first-release date are recorded as contextual metadata only and are not scored.

citations: This is embodied by our use of a “release train” model, in which we issue a new release every 6 weeks.
A new stable release is produced every six weeks.
documented_cadence.rationale: Rust has shipped on a strict, publicly documented 6-week 'release train' since 1.0 (2015): stable, beta and nightly channels move in lockstep, and a new stable release is produced every six weeks.

citations: Only the latest stable release receives patches.
Ultimately, it is also a question of “how much effort would this be to maintain and what are the benefits?”
trade-off for why the Rust project itself does not maintain one (or many!?)
maintenance_cadence.rationale: Releases are frequent and predictable, but Rust deliberately has no official long-term-support branch: only the single latest stable release receives patches, so users needing patched older versions must rely on distro or third-party backports; this is a documented, intentional trade-off rather than an oversight.

citations: The Rust programming language uses deterministic versioning for toolchain releases.
Stable versions use SemVer, while nightly, beta and historical builds can be accessed by using dated builds (YY-MM-DD).
reproducible_artifacts.rationale: Rust toolchain releases use deterministic SemVer versioning and every historical stable/beta/nightly build is retrievable from static.rust-lang.org archives, supporting reproducible installs and historical crater-style compatibility analysis.

citations: The stable release channel will provide pain-free upgrades, and the nightly channel will give early adopters access to unfinished features as we work on them.

Its primary purpose is to detect regressions in the Rust compiler, and it does this by building a large number of crates, running their test suites and comparing the results between two versions of the Rust compiler.
stability_commitment.rationale: Rust's 2014 'Stability as a Deliverable' commitment underlies the stable channel's pain-free upgrade guarantee, and this is mechanically enforced pre-release by Crater, which builds and tests a large fraction of published crates against beta/nightly builds to catch regressions before they reach stable.

citations: Rust uses editions to make backwards-incompatible changes.
Editions are skin-deep, and as a result - you can always use an older edition alongside a supported version of the compiler.
Editions are expected to be released every three years.
The MSRV defines the oldest Rust compiler version that your project guarantees to work with.
versioning_support_policy.rationale: Rust uses SemVer for compiler releases and an opt-in Edition mechanism (targeted at roughly a three-year cadence) for backward-incompatible surface changes; editions are 'skin deep' so old and new edition code interoperate under one compiler, and crates declare an explicit MSRV contract via Cargo.toml.
